parts.text:
5
A ball is kicked upwards at an angle of 45° to horizontal ground. After a short flight, the ball
returns to the ground.
It may be assumed that air resistance is negligible.
What is never zero during the flight of the ball?
A
the horizontal component of the ball’s acceleration
B
the horizontal component of the ball’s velocity
C
the vertical component of the ball’s momentum
D
the vertical component of the ball’s velocity

hints: Notice the ball is launched at $45^\circ$, so it starts with both a forward horizontal velocity and an upward vertical velocity.
With air resistance negligible, there is no horizontal force on the ball, so think about what that implies for horizontal acceleration and horizontal velocity.
Track the vertical motion up to maximum height and back down, and ask which vertical quantity must pass through zero at the top.
walkthrough: Identify the projectile conditions: launch at $45^\circ$ gives initial components $v_x = v\cos 45^\circ$ and $v_y = v\sin 45^\circ$, both non-zero, with only weight acting vertically.
State the governing rule: with air resistance negligible, horizontal force is zero so horizontal acceleration $a_x = 0$, while vertical acceleration is $a_y = -g$ throughout flight.
Apply this to horizontal motion: $a_x = 0$ at all times, so $v_x$ remains constant at its initial positive value and never changes to zero.
Apply this to vertical motion: $v_y$ starts positive, decreases at rate $g$, becomes zero instantaneously at maximum height, then becomes negative on descent.
Link momentum to velocity: vertical momentum $p_y = mv_y$ must also be zero when $v_y$ is zero at the top.
Therefore only the constant non-zero horizontal velocity is never zero. This is option B.

A.explanation: With no air resistance there is no horizontal force, so horizontal acceleration is always zero, not never zero.

B.explanation: Horizontal velocity stays constant at $v \cos 45^\circ > 0$ because there is no horizontal acceleration, so it never reaches zero.

C.explanation: Vertical momentum is $mv_y$ and $v_y$ is zero at maximum height, so it is zero once during flight.

D.explanation: Vertical velocity decreases to zero at the top of the 45-degree trajectory before becoming negative, so it is zero once.
